analysis.one_liner: Requires taxpayers earning over $1 million to pay at least 30% of income in federal taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 Senate cosponsors, was referred to the Finance Committee and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone with adjusted gross income above $1 million to pay a minimum of 30% of that income (after charitable deductions) in federal taxes. Any amount they owe beyond their existing income tax, alternative minimum tax, and payroll tax would become a new 'fair share tax,' with a phased-in rate and an inflation-adjusted threshold. The bill's stated purpose is deficit reduction, and it includes a non-binding statement that Congress should pursue broader tax reform closing loopholes for the wealthy.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 99.9% of taxpayers earning under $1 million, whose tax bills would not change while the wealthiest households pay more; and all federal taxpayers to the extent the added revenue reduces deficits.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a minimum 30% tax rate on adjusted gross income above $1 million (after charitable deductions), so high earners cannot pay a lower effective rate than many middle-income families.
Counts the income tax, alternative minimum tax, and payroll tax a millionaire already pays toward the 30% floor, so it tops up existing liability rather than stacking a second full tax.
States a purpose of cutting the deficit by billions of dollars a year, and preserves the full relative value of charitable contribution deductions for high earners who itemize.
Indexes the $1 million threshold to inflation after 2013, so the tax does not gradually capture more of the upper-middle class over time.
Phases the tax in gradually for taxpayers just above the $1 million line, avoiding a sharp cliff.

analysis.who_pays: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million — about the top one-tenth of one percent of earners — who currently pay combined federal rates below 30% because much of their income is investment income or otherwise taxed at preferential rates.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises money on the scale of billions a year, which is a small fraction of the federal deficit, and its own text describes it as an interim step awaiting broader tax reform rather than a solution.

The tax applies only to the gap between 30% of income and what a taxpayer already owes in income tax, the alternative minimum tax, and payroll tax, so millionaires who already pay at least 30% owe nothing more.

It leaves the underlying tax loopholes that let high earners pay low rates untouched, and instead patches over them with a floor — a simpler alternative would be closing the loopholes directly, which the bill's own 'sense of the Senate' section calls for but does not enact.
The 30% floor on very high incomes could reduce incentives to realize investment income in some cases, a standard trade-off of any rate increase at the top.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted fix: it forces a small group of very high earners to pay an effective rate comparable to what middle-income wage earners pay, while preserving charitable giving and phasing in at the threshold. Its honest weakness is scale — it raises meaningful but modest revenue and does not close the loopholes it highlights, so it is more a statement of principle with real money attached than a structural tax reform.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 1, 2012, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 1, 2012, joined by eight original cosponsors including Senators Sanders, Schumer, Harkin, and Leahy.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
The complete action history shows no further action after the referral — the Finance Committee never considered the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor.
All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on.
In the same session, the Senate's only vote on a companion Buffett Rule bill failed a procedural vote 51-48, short of the 60 needed to move forward.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning over $1 million, who kept paying the lower effective rates the bill would have eliminated, and the Senate Finance Committee's leadership, which avoided a vote that would have put senators on record on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who kept paying less

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 1, 2012 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 11 senators (10 Democrats, 1 independent)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 11 were Democrats or independents.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Made the 'Buffett Rule' — the 30% minimum tax on millionaires this bill embodied — a centerpiece of his 2012 agenda and pressed Congress to pass it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Max Baucus)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; chair sets its agenda
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote ever appeared in its action history.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the Buffett Rule and voted unanimously against a procedural vote to advance the companion bill in April 2012, which failed 51-48, short of the 60 needed.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 11 cosponsors was a Democrat or independent, no Republican cosponsored it, and the Senate's only vote on the companion Buffett Rule bill split along party lines, 51-48.

industries.industry: Households with adjusted gross income over $1 million
industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on roughly the top one-tenth of one percent of earners, who would owe the gap between what they pay now and 30% of income. Their interest in the bill's failure runs directly against deficit reduction and against middle-income taxpayers who pay a larger share of income in payroll taxes.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: Fund managers whose income is taxed at preferential capital-gains-type rates are the clearest case of earners paying far below 30%; the bill would top their liability up to the floor. Their income sits above the pay structures of ordinary wage earners, which is the fairness gap the bill targets.

The bill carves out charitable contribution deductions, scaled to their full relative value, so it is designed not to discourage large donations. Charitable groups lose nothing under the bill's structure.
